title: Admission control and rate limiting
subtitle: Every surface I expose has a stated limit and a typed refusal.

stats.label: for every admission limit, so a new one is watched before it refuses
processes, agent calls, a scheduler and a poller, on one account-wide X limit
platform usage past which the Facebook poller skips its run
daily caps of my own on the social modules

lede: I built admission control into the memory service, the execution substrate's admission controller and a GPU decoder that refuses with a number rather than queueing silently. I decide where a limit sits by asking what the protected resource actually runs out of. FAFO Core and Function Forge lets agents call database-heavy functions over MCP, and agents submit as much work as you let them. The database has a fixed number of connections, a fixed write budget and fixed I/O, and the operations behind those functions range from zero-write reads to rewrites of a whole vector lattice. One request-per-second limit cannot fit that range.
quote: A refusal carries a type and a number the caller can act on; a silent queue or a timeout gives the caller nothing.
evidence: Database admission control: a Rust admission service that prices each request by its expected cost to the database, so heavy rewrites wait and cheap reads flow, with off, shadow and enforcing modes.

Rate limiting for third-party APIs: Redis buckets on the server's clock, reads refused when a rolling budget is spent and writes paced, never rejected; one service owning a limit shared by 3 processes.
API quota sharing: a Facebook module that returns the platform's usage headers with every tool result and skips background polls past 60 percent usage, leaving room for agents.

Backpressure with typed refusal: a GPU tool-discovery decoder that admits work against measured free memory beside a serving model and answers a full engine with a typed busy response and a retry hint.
author: Corey James
